filename: Senior Living Research Digest — Cognitive Decline — June 2026.md
title: Senior Living Research Digest — Cognitive Decline — June 2026
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Higher Resting Heart Rate Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed data from 19,114 community-dwelling adults aged 65+ without cardiovascular disease or dementia who participated in the ASPREE trial. Resting heart rate was measured at baseline and follow-up visits. Compared to those with heart rates of 60-69 bpm, participants with rates of 80+ bpm had a 9% higher risk of cognitive decline. When researchers looked at average heart rate over five years, rates of 70-79 bpm and 80+ bpm were associated with 10% and 16% higher cognitive decline risks, respectively.
studies.why_it_matters: Resting heart rate is a simple, free measurement that could help identify older adults at increased risk for cognitive problems—potentially years before symptoms appear.
studies.story_angle_primary: Your resting heart rate may offer clues about brain health. Consider asking your doctor about your heart rate trends at your next checkup—it's information you can track yourself and discuss as part of your overall wellness picture.
studies.story_angle_secondary: For senior living communities, routine vital sign monitoring already captures heart rate data. This research suggests these existing measurements could be incorporated into early cognitive screening protocols.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation); secondary analysis of a trial designed for other purposes.

studies.title: Daily Step Counts Track with Cognitive Status in People with Alzheimer's Disease
studies.the_study: Researchers equipped 70 participants—including 19 with Alzheimer's dementia, 28 with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's, and 23 cognitively healthy older adults—with Samsung Galaxy smartwatches for approximately one week. Those with Alzheimer's dementia showed significantly reduced step counts and lower walking intensity compared to both other groups. Importantly, step metrics correlated with cognitive test performance.
studies.why_it_matters: Commercial smartwatches may provide a practical, low-cost way to monitor everyday functioning in people with Alzheimer's disease without requiring clinic visits.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a loved one has memory concerns, a simple fitness tracker may provide useful information about daily activity levels to share with healthcare providers—though it's not a diagnostic tool.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Families and memory care staff could use smartwatch data to track changes in mobility patterns over time, potentially catching functional decline earlier than periodic assessments alone.
studies.caveats: Small sample size (N=70); cross-sectional design limits causal conclusions; single-center study.

studies.title: Electrical Nerve Stimulation Combined with Exercise Improves Cognition After Stroke
studies.the_study: In this randomized controlled trial, 90 people with chronic stroke (average age 65) received 18 sessions over six weeks of either transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS), transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS), or sham stimulation—all combined with upper limb exercises. Both active stimulation groups showed significantly greater improvements in cognitive scores (Montreal Cognitive Assessment) compared to sham, with gains persisting one month later.
studies.why_it_matters: For stroke survivors experiencing both cognitive and physical challenges, combining electrical stimulation with rehabilitation exercises may offer dual benefits.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've had a stroke, ask your rehabilitation team about newer approaches like nerve stimulation that might enhance your recovery exercises—this research suggests combination therapies may work better than exercise alone.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Rehabilitation facilities and senior living communities with therapy programs may want to explore adding transcutaneous nerve stimulation devices, which are non-invasive and relatively affordable.
studies.caveats: Single-center study; participants knew which treatment they received (not fully blinded); follow-up limited to one month.

studies.title: Brain Stimulation Shows Promise for Memory in Mild Cognitive Impairment
studies.the_study: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined 22 studies (826 total participants aged 60+) testing transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) for cognitive improvement. Overall, tACS showed a moderate beneficial effect on cognition. The most consistent benefits appeared in people with mild cognitive impairment, particularly for memory, where effects were homogeneous across studies.
studies.why_it_matters: Non-invasive brain stimulation could become a tool for supporting memory in the earliest stages of cognitive decline, when intervention may be most effective.
studies.story_angle_primary: Brain stimulation techniques are being studied as potential memory aids—while not yet standard treatment, this growing research area may eventually offer new options for those with early memory concerns.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Memory clinics and research centers may increasingly offer tACS as part of clinical trials; families should know this is an emerging area worth monitoring.
studies.caveats: High heterogeneity in methods across studies; effects varied considerably in healthy older adults and those with dementia; clinical translation not yet established.

studies.title: Moderate-to-Vigorous Exercise May Protect Against Amyloid-Related Cognitive Decline
studies.the_study: Researchers followed 74 community-dwelling older adults (average age 73) who underwent brain amyloid PET scans and cognitive testing over nearly two years. Among those with elevated brain amyloid (a hallmark of Alzheimer's pathology), higher levels of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (150+ minutes/week) were associated with significantly less cognitive decline. Notably, lighter walking activity did not show this protective association.
studies.why_it_matters: For people who may already have Alzheimer's-related brain changes, getting enough vigorous activity—not just gentle walking—may help preserve cognitive function.
studies.story_angle_primary: This research suggests that brisk walking, swimming, cycling, or other activities that get your heart pumping may offer brain benefits beyond gentler exercise—aim for at least 150 minutes weekly of activity that makes you breathe harder.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior fitness programs might consider emphasizing moderate-intensity options alongside gentler activities, particularly for residents concerned about cognitive health.
studies.caveats: Small sample size (N=74); observational design; physical activity was self-reported; relatively short follow-up period.

studies.title: Hearing Aids May Help Delay Cognitive Decline—Here's Why It Matters
studies.the_study: This comprehensive review examines the relationship between hearing loss and dementia risk. Hearing impairment affects roughly one-third of adults over 65 and has been identified as a potentially modifiable risk factor for dementia. The authors explain that hearing loss may accelerate cognitive decline by increasing mental effort required for listening, reducing social engagement, and promoting isolation.
studies.why_it_matters: Correcting hearing loss with hearing aids may be one of the most accessible interventions available to reduce dementia risk.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've been putting off getting your hearing checked or wearing hearing aids, this research adds another important reason to act—protecting your hearing may help protect your thinking abilities too.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living communities should consider routine hearing screenings and ensuring residents have access to audiological services and properly fitted hearing aids.
studies.caveats: Narrative review (not systematic); causation between hearing loss and dementia not definitively established.

studies.title: Pain Intensity and Interference Both Linked to Cognitive Problems in Older Adults
studies.the_study: Among 1,343 older adults (average age 70) in Iran, researchers found that both pain severity and how much pain interfered with daily activities were significantly associated with cognitive impairment after adjusting for other factors. Nearly 60% of participants showed signs of cognitive impairment on standardized tests.
studies.why_it_matters: Addressing chronic pain in older adults isn't just about comfort—it may also support cognitive health.
studies.story_angle_primary: If chronic pain is limiting your daily activities, working with your doctor to manage it better may benefit not just your quality of life but potentially your mental sharpness as well.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Care providers should recognize that untreated or undertreated pain in older residents may contribute to cognitive difficulties; comprehensive pain management deserves attention as part of brain health strategies.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design (cannot determine if pain causes cognitive problems or vice versa); single geographic region may limit generalizability.

studies.title: Music Therapy Supports Cognitive Function and Reduces Depression in Healthy Older Adults
studies.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences
studies.the_study: In this randomized controlled trial, 62 older adults without cognitive impairment (average age ~80) were assigned to receive structured music therapy either one-on-one, in small groups, or in large groups over 20 weeks, while a control group received no music therapy. All three music therapy formats showed improvements in memory, attention, executive function, and depressive symptoms compared to controls, whose cognitive scores actually declined over the study period.
studies.why_it_matters: Structured music therapy—regardless of group size—may help maintain cognitive function and mood in healthy older adults.
studies.story_angle_primary: Participating in structured music activities isn't just enjoyable—it may help keep your mind sharp. Look for music therapy programs or even regular music groups in your community.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living activity directors have evidence that music therapy programs, whether individual or group-based, can support residents' cognitive and emotional well-being.
studies.caveats: Control group received no intervention (not an active control); participants knew their group assignment; relatively small sample.

studies.title: Frailty and Advanced Age Strongly Predict Both Cognitive Decline and Mortality
studies.the_study: Researchers tracked 1,413 community-dwelling older adults in Brazil for nine years using cognitive assessments. During follow-up, 51% experienced cognitive decline. Frailty tripled the odds of cognitive decline and quadrupled mortality risk. Adults aged 80+ had five times the odds of cognitive decline and nearly 12 times the mortality risk compared to younger participants. Having prior cognitive problems strongly predicted subsequent decline.
studies.why_it_matters: Frailty and age together create compound risk—identifying and addressing frailty may be key to preserving both cognitive function and life expectancy.
studies.story_angle_primary: Staying physically strong and addressing early signs of frailty—like weakness, fatigue, or unintentional weight loss—may help protect your thinking abilities as you age.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Routine frailty assessments in senior care settings could help identify individuals who need more intensive cognitive monitoring and intervention.
studies.caveats: Single-country sample; used AI for English editing; observational design.

studies.title: Functional Disabilities Predict Housing Transitions—Cognitive Decline Drives Nursing Home Placement
studies.journal: The Journal of Frailty and Aging
studies.the_study: Following 5,264 French older adults (average age 75) for up to 30 years, researchers tracked transitions from home to intermediate housing or nursing homes. Mild to moderate disability was associated with moves to both settings, while severe disability and cognitive impairment specifically predicted nursing home admission. Difficulty with transportation predicted moves for women, while medication management difficulties predicted nursing home placement for men.
studies.why_it_matters: Different types of functional difficulties predict different housing outcomes—understanding these patterns can help families plan ahead.
studies.story_angle_primary: Maintaining your ability to manage medications, handle finances, and get around independently may be key to staying in your preferred living situation longer.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Families should monitor specific daily living skills—particularly medication management, shopping, and transportation—as early warning signs that more support may be needed.
studies.caveats: French population; observational design; intermediate housing options may differ across countries.

studies.title: Higher Pulse Pressure Speeds Cognitive Decline—But Only When Blood Pressure Is Elevated
studies.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences
studies.the_study: Analyzing data from 2,787 older adults (average age 74) over 10 years, researchers found that higher pulse pressure (the difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure) predicted faster cognitive decline in global cognition, memory, and reasoning. Importantly, this effect was only seen in those with elevated blood pressure—pulse pressure didn't affect cognition in people with normal blood pressure.
studies.why_it_matters: For older adults with high blood pressure, monitoring pulse pressure may provide additional insight into cognitive risk.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have high blood pressure, ask your doctor about your pulse pressure (the gap between your top and bottom numbers)—keeping blood pressure controlled may help protect your brain.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living health staff monitoring blood pressure should note pulse pressure as an additional metric worth tracking, particularly for residents with hypertension.
studies.caveats: Observational design; secondary analysis of trial data; pulse pressure is influenced by many factors.

studies.title: Gamified Hearing-and-Brain Training Shows Promise for Older Adults with Hearing Loss
studies.the_study: In this pilot randomized controlled trial, 60 community-dwelling older adults (average age 68) with mild-to-moderate hearing loss either used a web-based auditory-cognitive training program or were placed on a waitlist. The training group showed significant improvements in focused and divided attention, as well as specific cognitive skills like naming and visual cognition. Participants found the program acceptable and reported benefits in self-awareness and information processing.
studies.why_it_matters: Home-based digital training combining hearing and cognitive exercises could be an accessible way to support brain health in people with hearing loss.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss, computer or tablet-based training programs that exercise both your hearing and thinking skills may offer benefits you can pursue from home—ask your audiologist about available options.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living technology programs could consider adding auditory-cognitive training apps to their offerings, particularly for residents with hearing difficulties.
studies.caveats: Small pilot study; waitlist control (no active comparison); relatively short intervention period.

studies.title: Socioeconomic Disadvantage Across Life Linked to Subjective Cognitive Decline
studies.journal: The Journals of Gerontology: Psychological Sciences
studies.the_study: Researchers examined two multi-ethnic cohorts of older adults (long-term Kaiser Permanente members without dementia) and found that lower financial, social, and cultural resources—both in childhood and later life—were independently associated with more self-reported cognitive decline. Depression partially explained these associations, accounting for 34-64% of the link between socioeconomic disadvantage and cognitive complaints.
studies.why_it_matters: Life circumstances throughout the lifespan influence cognitive health in older age—and treating depression may help break this cycle.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're noticing memory changes and also feeling down, addressing depression with your doctor may help improve both your mood and your perception of your thinking abilities.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior services should recognize that older adults who faced socioeconomic hardship—whether in childhood or currently—may benefit from enhanced cognitive and mental health support.
studies.caveats: Self-reported cognitive decline (not objective testing); observational design; specific populations may limit generalizability.

studies.title: Antioxidant-Rich Lifestyle Plus Good Sleep May Protect Against Cognitive Impairment
studies.journal: The Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging
studies.the_study: Among 4,988 adults aged 60+ in rural China followed for 10 years, researchers found that a higher "oxidative balance score" (reflecting antioxidant-rich diet and healthy lifestyle) was associated with lower odds of cognitive impairment. Both short (<6 hours) and long (>8 hours) sleep were linked to higher cognitive impairment risk. Certain combinations—like short sleep with moderate antioxidant intake—showed particularly elevated risk.
studies.why_it_matters: Diet, lifestyle, and sleep work together to influence brain health—optimizing all three may provide the greatest protection.
studies.story_angle_primary: A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and other antioxidants, combined with getting 7-8 hours of sleep nightly, may work together to help keep your mind sharp as you age.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior dining programs emphasizing antioxidant-rich foods, combined with attention to residents' sleep quality, may support cognitive health more effectively than focusing on either alone.
studies.caveats: Single geographic region (rural China); observational design; sleep duration was self-reported.

studies.title: Sarcopenia and Sarcopenic Obesity Substantially Increase Dementia Risk
studies.journal: The Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging
studies.the_study: Following over 420,000 UK Biobank participants for nearly 14 years, researchers found that sarcopenia (muscle loss) and particularly sarcopenic obesity (muscle loss combined with obesity) significantly increased dementia risk. Those with sarcopenic obesity had 69% higher risk of all-cause dementia compared to those with neither condition. The associations held for both Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia.
studies.why_it_matters: Maintaining muscle mass while managing weight may be a powerful strategy for reducing dementia risk.
studies.story_angle_primary: Preserving your muscle strength through resistance exercises and adequate protein intake matters for your brain as well as your body—especially if you're also carrying extra weight.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living fitness and nutrition programs should prioritize muscle-building activities and protein-rich diets, recognizing that sarcopenia prevention may also be dementia prevention.
studies.caveats: UK population; sarcopenia defined by grip strength and muscle mass estimates (not clinical diagnosis); observational design.

studies.title: Digital Health Tools Can Help Combat Loneliness in Older Adults
studies.the_study: This comprehensive review examined digital health interventions for loneliness in older adults, including video visits, telephone programs, group videoconferencing, mental health apps, and social robots. While results varied, several approaches showed meaningful reductions in loneliness, depression, and anxiety. However, the "digital divide"—limited access to technology and digital literacy—remains a significant barrier to equitable implementation.
studies.why_it_matters: Technology can help connect isolated older adults, but requires attention to accessibility and training to be effective.
studies.story_angle_primary: Video calls, telephone check-ins, and even social robot companions can help reduce feelings of loneliness—don't hesitate to ask family or community resources for help learning to use these tools.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living communities implementing telehealth and social technology programs need to invest in training and technical support, not just equipment, to ensure all residents can benefit.
studies.caveats: Narrative review; heterogeneous study quality; evidence strength varies across interventions.

studies.title: GLP-1 Diabetes Medications Linked to Better Vascular Cell Levels and Cognition
studies.the_study: In 154 adults with type 2 diabetes aged 60-80, researchers found that higher levels of angiogenic T cells (cells that help repair blood vessels) were associated with better cognitive performance. After matching for age, weight, and blood sugar control, those taking GLP-1 receptor agonists (like semaglutide or liraglutide) plus metformin had significantly higher levels of these beneficial cells compared to those on metformin alone.
studies.why_it_matters: Popular diabetes medications may have cognitive benefits beyond blood sugar control, potentially through effects on blood vessel health.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have diabetes, discuss with your doctor whether newer medications like GLP-1 receptor agonists might be appropriate for you—they may offer benefits beyond blood sugar control.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Healthcare providers managing diabetes in older adults should be aware of emerging evidence suggesting cognitive benefits of GLP-1 medications, though this wasn't a randomized trial.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design (cannot prove causation); relatively small sample after matching; single-center study.

studies.title: Calcium Supplements May Increase Cognitive Decline Risk in Older Women
studies.the_study: Following 227 cognitively healthy French women (average age 80) for seven years, researchers found that those taking calcium supplements at baseline had more than three times the risk of cognitive decline compared to non-users, even after adjusting for age, obesity, physical activity, diet, and health conditions. About 26% of all participants experienced cognitive decline during follow-up.
studies.why_it_matters: While calcium is important for bone health, supplementation may carry unexpected cognitive risks that deserve consideration.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before taking calcium supplements, discuss with your doctor whether you truly need them and whether dietary sources might be sufficient—this study raises questions about supplement safety for brain health.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior care providers and families should review calcium supplementation with healthcare providers, considering the balance of bone health benefits against potential cognitive concerns.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation); single-center study in France; relatively small sample; women only.

studies.title: App-Based Sleep and Memory Assessment Feasible for Older Adults with Memory Concerns
studies.the_study: Researchers tested a smartphone app called "Sleep Memories" that assesses overnight memory consolidation in 76 older adults (average age 70) with subjective cognitive decline or mild cognitive impairment. Over half completed both evening and morning memory tests, and users generally found the app acceptable. Lower willingness to participate was associated with poorer cognition and worse sleep habits.
studies.why_it_matters: Home-based memory assessment apps may provide clinically useful information for people at risk of cognitive decline, though engagement varies by individual characteristics.
studies.story_angle_primary: Sleep plays an important role in memory—apps that test how well you remember information after sleep may someday help identify memory concerns earlier.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Memory clinics may increasingly use home-based digital tools to supplement in-office assessments, though patients with worse cognition may need extra support to participate.
studies.caveats: Pilot feasibility study (not designed to test clinical effectiveness); some technical difficulties reported; participants from specialized memory clinic.

studies.title: Digital Handwriting Analysis Detects Subtle Cognitive Changes in Community-Dwelling Older Adults
studies.the_study: Among 174 community-dwelling adults aged 60+ (average age 74), those who had difficulty copying a simple pentagon drawing showed significantly different handwriting patterns when tested digitally—specifically longer writing times and lower pressure. These digital handwriting differences were detected even when standard physical performance tests didn't distinguish between groups.
studies.why_it_matters: Simple digital writing tasks could provide sensitive, non-invasive screening for subtle cognitive changes in community settings.
studies.story_angle_primary: How you write—not just what you write—may reveal early changes in brain function. Future screening might involve simple writing tasks on a tablet.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior centers and primary care offices may eventually use tablet-based handwriting analysis as an easy, quick screening tool during routine visits.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional design; pentagon-copying performance used as proxy for cognitive status (not clinical diagnosis); single geographic region.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — June 2026
**Checked:** 2026-06-27 | **Studies reviewed:** 20
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

# Fact-Check Report

### Study 1: Higher Resting Heart Rate Linked to Faster Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
**PMID:** 42329536 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. The digest correctly reports the sample size (N=19,114), population (community-dwelling adults aged 65+ without cardiovascular disease or dementia), the ASPREE trial source, and the key findings (9% higher risk at 80+ bpm baseline; 10% and 16% higher risks at 70-79 and 80+ bpm for 5-year average). Observational design caveat appropriately noted.

---

### Study 2: Daily Step Counts Track with Cognitive Status in People with Alzheimer's Disease
**PMID:** 42340575 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample breakdown (19 ADD, 28 ADMCI, 23 cognitively unimpaired) correctly totals 70. Samsung Galaxy smartwatch detail, approximately one-week monitoring period, and findings about step counts correlating with cognitive test performance are all accurate. Cross-sectional limitation appropriately flagged.

---

### Study 3: Electrical Nerve Stimulation Combined with Exercise Improves Cognition After Stroke
**PMID:** 42287562 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Blinding characterization** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "participants knew which treatment they received (not fully blinded)"
- **Abstract says:** The abstract does not explicitly state whether blinding was successful or failed; it only describes study design as an RCT with sham stimulation.
- **Problem:** The caveat implies known unblinding, but this is an inference not directly supported by the abstract text. However, given that tVNS/tSCS involve perceptible sensations, this is a reasonable assumption.
- **Suggested fix:** No revision required, but could soften to: "Single-blind design with sham control; blinding effectiveness not reported."

All other facts (N=90, mean age 65.12, 18 sessions over 6 weeks, three groups, MoCA and FMAUE outcomes, 1-month follow-up, single-center) are accurate.

---

### Study 4: Brain Stimulation Shows Promise for Memory in Mild Cognitive Impairment
**PMID:** 42313252 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. The digest correctly reports this as a systematic review and meta-analysis, 22 studies with 826 participants aged 60+, moderate beneficial effect (g=0.70), homogeneous effects in MCI (I²=0%), and memory as most responsive domain. High heterogeneity caveat appropriately noted.

---

### Study 5: Moderate-to-Vigorous Exercise May Protect Against Amyloid-Related Cognitive Decline
**PMID:** 42185590 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Follow-up period description** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "over nearly two years"
- **Abstract says:** "mean interval = 23.6 ± 0.9 months"
- **Problem:** 23.6 months is closer to 2 years than "nearly two years" suggests; this is accurate but could be more precise.
- **Suggested fix:** "over approximately two years (mean 23.6 months)"

**Issue B. Amyloid positivity threshold** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "elevated brain amyloid (a hallmark of Alzheimer's pathology)"
- **Abstract says:** "Aβ positivity was defined as a global standardized uptake value ratio > 1.10"
- **Problem:** The digest's characterization is accurate for lay audience; no correction needed.

All key facts (N=74, mean age 72.7, 24.3% Aβ positive, MVPA threshold 150+ min/week, no walking effect) are accurate. Self-reported physical activity caveat appropriately noted.

---

### Study 6: Hearing Aids May Help Delay Cognitive Decline—Here's Why It Matters
**PMID:** 42252380 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Prevalence statistic source** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Hearing impairment affects roughly one-third of adults over 65"
- **Abstract says:** "Cognitive impairment is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide and it affects about 6.5% of the population over the age of 65"
- **Problem:** The abstract states cognitive impairment affects 6.5% over 65, but does not provide a specific prevalence for hearing impairment. The "one-third" figure is not verifiable from the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** Either remove the statistic or flag as "Unverifiable from abstract only."

All other content (narrative review characterization, mechanisms described, hearing aids recommendation) is consistent with the abstract. Review type caveat appropriately noted.

---

### Study 7: Pain Intensity and Interference Both Linked to Cognitive Problems in Older Adults
**PMID:** 42201471 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample size (N=1,343), mean age (69.73), location (Iran/Birjand), cognitive impairment prevalence (59.64%), and findings about both pain severity and pain interference being significantly associated with cognitive impairment are all accurate. Cross-sectional design caveat appropriately noted.

---

### Study 8: Music Therapy Supports Cognitive Function and Reduces Depression in Healthy Older Adults
**PMID:** 42161569 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample size (N=62), RCT design, 20-week intervention, three MT formats plus passive control, mean ages (ranging 74.56-82.00), findings about cognitive improvements and depression reduction, and control group cognitive decline are all accurately reported. Caveats about passive control and unblinding appropriately noted.

---

### Study 9: Frailty and Advanced Age Strongly Predict Both Cognitive Decline and Mortality
**PMID:** 42268499 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Frailty odds ratio precision** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Frailty tripled the odds of cognitive decline"
- **Abstract says:** "Frailty increased the odds of both cognitive deficit (OR = 3.1; 95% CI 1.86-5.18)"
- **Problem:** OR of 3.1 is more precisely "tripled" but the digest's phrasing is acceptable for lay audience.

**Issue B. Mortality odds ratio** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "quadrupled mortality risk"
- **Abstract says:** "mortality (OR = 4.2; 95% CI 2.66-6.69)"
- **Problem:** OR of 4.2 is slightly more than quadrupled; this is acceptable rounding for lay audience.

All other facts (N=1,413, Brazil, 9 years, 51% cognitive decline, age 80+ OR=5.2 for decline and OR=11.9 for mortality) are accurate. AI editing caveat appropriately noted per abstract disclosure.

---

### Study 10: Functional Disabilities Predict Housing Transitions—Cognitive Decline Drives Nursing Home Placement
**PMID:** 42177766 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample size (N=5,264), mean age (74.7), follow-up (up to 30 years, median 10.2 years), French population, findings about disability severity predicting different housing types, and sex-specific findings (transportation for women, medication management for men) are all accurate. Observational design caveat appropriately noted.

---

### Study 11: Higher Pulse Pressure Speeds Cognitive Decline—But Only When Blood Pressure Is Elevated
**PMID:** 42178211 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sample size discrepancy** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "2,787 older adults"
- **Abstract says:** "We used data from the ACTIVE trial (N = 2,802 adults aged 65+)" and later "Among 2,787 older adults"
- **Problem:** The digest uses 2,787 which matches the analytic sample; this is correct.

All other facts (mean age 73.65, 10 years, findings about pulse pressure and blood pressure interaction, cognitive domains) are accurate. Observational design and secondary analysis caveats appropriately noted.

---

### Study 12: Gamified Hearing-and-Brain Training Shows Promise for Older Adults with Hearing Loss
**PMID:** 42302249 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample size (N=60), mean age (67.65), mild-to-moderate hearing loss population, pilot RCT design, waitlist control, findings about focused and divided attention improvements, and acceptability findings are all accurate. Caveats about pilot study and waitlist control appropriately noted.

---

### Study 13: Socioeconomic Disadvantage Across Life Linked to Subjective Cognitive Decline
**PMID:** 42289977 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Two multi-ethnic cohorts of Kaiser Permanente members without dementia, findings about childhood and late-life SES measures, depression mediation (34-64%), and ECog-12 scale use are all accurate. Self-reported cognitive decline and observational design caveats appropriately noted.

---

### Study 14: Antioxidant-Rich Lifestyle Plus Good Sleep May Protect Against Cognitive Impairment
**PMID:** 42241923 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sleep duration thresholds** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Both short (<6 hours) and long (>8 hours) sleep"
- **Abstract says:** The abstract does not specify the exact cutoff values for short and long sleep duration.
- **Problem:** The specific thresholds (<6 and >8 hours) are not verifiable from the abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Both short and long sleep duration (compared to normal) were linked to higher cognitive impairment risk."

All other facts (N=4,988, age 60+, rural China, 10-year follow-up, 15.2% cognitive impairment, OBS findings, interaction analysis) are accurate. Observational design and self-reported sleep caveats appropriately noted.

---

### Study 15: Sarcopenia and Sarcopenic Obesity Substantially Increase Dementia Risk
**PMID:** 42155951 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample size (420,916), UK Biobank source, follow-up (median 13.69 years), sarcopenic obesity HR of 1.69 (which represents 69% higher risk as stated), and findings for Alzheimer's and vascular dementia subtypes are all accurate. Observational design and sarcopenia definition caveats appropriately noted.

---

### Study 16: Digital Health Tools Can Help Combat Loneliness in Older Adults
**PMID:** 42166076 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.
